treatment: One cycle BEP vs nerve-sparing RPLND
population: 382 patients with clinical stage I non-seminomatous germ-cell tumours
ci: P=.0033; tumour-specific survival 100% in both arms
benefitText: One cycle of BEP produced fewer recurrences than RPLND in this randomized trial: 1.15% vs 7.5%, an absolute reduction of 6.35 percentage points (NNT 16). Tumour-specific survival was 100% in both groups. NNT is based on recurrence by approximately 4.7 years.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the primary publication; RPLND carries operative morbidity while BEP carries chemotherapy-related toxicity
trial: German Testicular Cancer Study Group AH 01/94
clinicalQuestion: In stage I non-seminoma, does one cycle of BEP provide better disease control than RPLND?
refs: Wittekind C, et al. Urologe A. 2008;47:1065–1070.

treatment: Risk-adapted surveillance vs one cycle adjuvant BEP
population: 745 patients with clinical stage I non-seminomatous germ-cell tumours in a prospective SWENOTECA programme
endpoint: Relapse rate on surveillance according to vascular invasion
nnt: 4 for adjuvant BEP if applied to the vascular-invasion-positive group
relativeEffect: Surveillance relapse 41.7% with vascular invasion vs 13.2% without
ci: Prospective management programme; not a randomized comparison of BEP vs surveillance
benefitText: SWENOTECA demonstrated why pathology matters in stage I NSGCT: among patients managed with surveillance, relapse was 41.7% with vascular invasion versus 13.2% without it. Mature follow-up of one-cycle BEP showed 5-year relapse rates of about 3.2% with vascular invasion and 1.6% without. This study supports risk-adapted management rather than a causal NNT because treatment allocation was not randomized. NNT is therefore not assigned as a trial-level causal estimate.
nnH: Not quantifiable from this nonrandomized programme; chemotherapy burden should be discussed against relapse risk
trial: SWENOTECA clinical stage I NSGCT management programme
clinicalQuestion: Does vascular invasion identify patients with sufficiently high relapse risk to justify adjuvant BEP in stage I non-seminoma?
refs: Tandstad T, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2009;27:2122–2128.
Tandstad T, et al. Ann Oncol. 2014;25:2167–2173.

treatment: Two CT scans vs five CT scans during surveillance
population: 414 patients with stage I NSGCT choosing surveillance
ci: 90% CI for difference -1.2% to 1.6%; no poor-prognosis relapses
benefitText: Reducing surveillance CT from five to two did not materially increase the proportion of relapses presenting with intermediate or poor prognosis: 0.8% vs 0.6%, difference 0.2 percentage points. No poor-prognosis relapse occurred. This supports less intensive CT surveillance and illustrates an Imaging setting rather than a treatment-efficacy question.
nnH: Not applicable as a clinical harm NNH; the relevant harm is cumulative radiation exposure and scan burden
clinicalQuestion: Can CT imaging be safely reduced during surveillance of stage I non-seminoma?
refs: Rustin GJ, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2007;25:1310–1315.

treatment: Tumour-marker decline guided dose-dense chemotherapy vs continued BEP in poor-prognosis NSGCT
population: 263 patients with IGCCCG poor-prognosis germ-cell tumours; 203 with unfavorable marker decline randomized
benefitText: Among patients with an unfavorable tumour-marker decline after one BEP cycle, switching to dose-dense intensified chemotherapy increased 5-year PFS from 46.7% to 58.9%, an absolute benefit of 12.2 points (NNT 9). Five-year OS was 70.9% vs 61.3%, HR 0.74, but this difference was not statistically significant. NNT is based on 5-year PFS.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the reported time-specific toxicity denominator; intensified treatment caused more neurotoxicity and hematologic toxicity
clinicalQuestion: Can early tumour-marker decline identify poor-prognosis GCT patients who benefit from intensified chemotherapy?
refs: Fizazi K, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2024;42:3270–3276.
Fizazi K, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2014;15:1442–1450.

treatment: Two cycles adjuvant BEP in high-risk stage I NSGCT
population: 114 eligible patients with high-risk clinical stage I NSGCT
nnt: 5 if compared with historical surveillance risk; not a randomized NNT
relativeEffect: 2 relapses among 104 histologically confirmed GCT patients
ci: 95% CI excluded a true relapse rate >5% in confirmed GCT
benefitText: Two cycles of BEP produced very low relapse rates in this prospective high-risk stage I cohort: only one relapse among 104 patients confirmed to have GCT on central pathology review. The study was not randomized, so a causal NNT cannot be assigned. It established the effectiveness of short-course cisplatin-based adjuvant therapy in a high-risk population.
nnH: Not quantifiable as an NNH; one treatment-related cerebrovascular death occurred and pulmonary-function changes were monitored
clinicalQuestion: Can short-course BEP substantially reduce relapse in high-risk stage I non-seminoma?
refs: Cullen MH, et al. J Clin Oncol. 1996;14:1093–1098.

treatment: Single-dose carboplatin followed by involved-node RT
population: 116 eligible patients with stage IIA or IIB classic seminoma
benefitText: A de-escalated regimen of one carboplatin cycle followed by involved-node RT achieved 93.7% 3-year PFS. The prespecified 95% target was not met, so this should be viewed as an investigational de-escalation strategy rather than proof of equivalence to standard RT or cisplatin-based chemotherapy. NNT is not applicable in a single-arm study.
nnH: Not applicable; single-arm study. Grade 3–4 events included neutropenia 4%, thrombocytopenia 3%, vomiting 1%
clinicalQuestion: Can stage IIA/IIB seminoma be treated with markedly de-escalated carboplatin plus involved-node RT?
refs: Papachristofilou A, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2022;23:1441–1450.

treatment: Neoadjuvant MVAC + radical cystectomy vs radical cystectomy alone
population: 307 evaluable patients with T2–T4a N0 M0 muscle-invasive bladder cancer
ci: 5-year OS P=.06; median OS 77 vs 46 months
benefitText: Neoadjuvant MVAC increased 5-year OS from 43% to 57%, an absolute benefit of 14 percentage points (NNT 8), with median OS 77 vs 46 months. Pathologic complete response was 38% vs 15%. NNT is based on 5-year overall survival.
nnH: Not quantifiable from the long-term publication; acute MVAC toxicity should be reported in text
clinicalQuestion: Does neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy improve survival before cystectomy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
refs: Grossman HB, et al. N Engl J Med. 2003;349:859–866.

treatment: Dose-dense MVAC vs gemcitabine-cisplatin before cystectomy
population: 493 patients with localized muscle-invasive bladder cancer eligible for cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy
relativeEffect: 0.77 for event-free survival in bladder/lymph-node population; OS difference modest
ci: Trial primarily demonstrated regimen differences in downstaging and event-free outcomes
benefitText: VESPER established that dose-dense MVAC is a reasonable intensive neoadjuvant regimen, with higher pathologic response and favorable event-free outcomes compared with gemcitabine-cisplatin. Five-year OS was about 71% vs 66%, an absolute difference of 5 points (NNT 20), but the principal value of the trial is regimen selection rather than a large OS effect. NNT is based on 5-year OS.
nnH: Not quantified here; ddMVAC has a different toxicity profile and requires growth-factor support
clinicalQuestion: Which cisplatin-based neoadjuvant regimen is preferable before cystectomy: ddMVAC or gemcitabine-cisplatin?
refs: Pfister C, et al. Eur Urol. 2022;82:165–176.

treatment: Adjuvant nivolumab vs placebo
population: 709 patients with high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma after radical resection
nnt: 9 for median-event reduction interpretation; fixed-time NNT requires a specified landmark
benefitText: At 3-year follow-up, median DFS was 22.0 months with nivolumab vs 10.9 months with placebo, HR 0.71. The original trial showed 6-month DFS 74.9% vs 60.3%, an absolute improvement of 14.6 points. A fixed-time NNT is therefore best based on the 6-month DFS landmark: NNT 7. The later median-based difference should not be converted into an NNT.
clinicalQuestion: Does adjuvant nivolumab reduce recurrence after radical surgery for high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma?
refs: Bajorin DF, et al. N Engl J Med. 2021;384:2102–2114.
Bajorin DF, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2025;43:15–21.

treatment: Adjuvant atezolizumab vs observation
population: 809 patients with high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma after radical surgery
nnt: Not applicable; no significant benefit demonstrated
benefitText: Atezolizumab did not improve DFS: median 19.4 vs 16.6 months, HR 0.89, P=.24. This negative phase III trial is important because it shows that adjuvant checkpoint inhibition cannot be assumed to work across all settings. NNT is not applicable because benefit was not demonstrated.
nnH: Not applicable as a comparative NNH because treatment-related grade 3–4 events were not reported for the observation arm
clinicalQuestion: Does adjuvant atezolizumab improve outcomes after surgery for high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma?
refs: Bellmunt J, et al. Lancet Oncol. 2021;22:525–537.

treatment: Avelumab maintenance + best supportive care vs best supportive care
population: 700 patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma without progression after 4–6 cycles of platinum chemotherapy
benefitText: One-year OS was 71.3% with avelumab maintenance vs 58.4% with best supportive care, an absolute benefit of 12.9 points (NNT 8). Median OS was 21.4 vs 14.3 months. NNT is based on 1-year overall survival.
clinicalQuestion: After disease control with first-line platinum chemotherapy, does maintenance avelumab improve survival?
refs: Powles T, et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;383:1218–1230.

treatment: Gemcitabine-cisplatin + nivolumab followed by nivolumab vs gemcitabine-cisplatin
population: 608 patients with previously untreated unresectable or metastatic urothelial carcinoma
nnt: Not appropriately calculable from median survival
benefitText: Median OS improved from 18.9 to 21.7 months, HR 0.78. At 12 months OS was 70.2% vs 62.7%, an absolute benefit of 7.5 points (NNT 14). NNT is based on 12-month overall survival, not the median survival difference.
clinicalQuestion: Does adding nivolumab to cisplatin-gemcitabine improve survival in untreated advanced urothelial carcinoma?
refs: van der Heijden MS, et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:1778–1789.

treatment: Perioperative durvalumab + neoadjuvant chemotherapy + adjuvant durvalumab vs neoadjuvant chemotherapy alone
population: 1,063 cisplatin-eligible patients with operable muscle-invasive bladder cancer
benefitText: Perioperative durvalumab improved 24-month EFS from 59.8% to 67.8%, an absolute benefit of 8 points (NNT 13). Twenty-four-month OS was also higher, 82.2% vs 75.2%, ARR 7 points. NNT is based on 24-month event-free survival.
nnH: Not applicable; the principal grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity rate was similar between groups
clinicalQuestion: Does perioperative durvalumab add meaningful benefit to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery in operable muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
refs: Powles T, et al. N Engl J Med. 2025;392:2367–2379.

treatment: Perioperative enfortumab vedotin + pembrolizumab + surgery vs surgery alone
population: 344 predominantly cisplatin-ineligible patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer
benefitText: Two-year EFS was 74.7% with perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab vs 39.4% with surgery alone, an absolute benefit of 35.3 points (NNT 3). Two-year OS was 79.7% vs 63.1%, ARR 16.6 points. NNT is based on 24-month EFS.
clinicalQuestion: In cisplatin-ineligible muscle-invasive bladder cancer, does perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab improve outcomes over surgery alone?
refs: Powles T, et al. N Engl J Med. 2026;394:144–156.

treatment: Adjuvant pembrolizumab vs placebo after nephrectomy
population: 994 patients with clear-cell RCC at intermediate-high or high risk of recurrence, including selected M1 NED
benefitText: At 72 months, DFS was 58.5% with pembrolizumab vs 48.7% with placebo, an absolute improvement of 9.8 points (NNT 11). Overall survival also favored pembrolizumab, HR 0.66, with 60-month OS 87.7% vs 82.3%. NNT is based on 72-month DFS.
nnH: Not quantified here; immune-related toxicity and treatment discontinuation should be reported separately
clinicalQuestion: Does adjuvant pembrolizumab reduce recurrence and improve survival after nephrectomy for high-risk RCC?
refs: Choueiri TK, et al. N Engl J Med. 2024;390:1359–1371.

treatment: Adjuvant nivolumab + ipilimumab vs placebo
population: 816 patients with high-risk clear-cell RCC after nephrectomy
benefitText: Adjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab did not improve DFS compared with placebo: HR 0.92, P=.53. Twenty-four-month DFS was 76.4% vs 74.0%, an absolute difference of only 2.4 points and not statistically significant. NNT is not assigned because benefit was not demonstrated.
harmLabel: Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events
clinicalQuestion: Does adjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab improve recurrence outcomes after nephrectomy for high-risk RCC?
refs: Motzer RJ, et al. N Engl J Med. 2022;386:683–694.

treatment: Adjuvant sorafenib for 1 or 3 years vs placebo
population: 1,711 patients with intermediate- or high-risk RCC after surgical excision
nnt: Not applicable; no DFS benefit demonstrated
benefitText: Three years of adjuvant sorafenib did not improve DFS compared with placebo: HR 1.01, P=.95. The restricted mean DFS difference was essentially zero. This is a key negative trial demonstrating that effective metastatic RCC TKIs should not automatically be transferred into the adjuvant setting. NNT is not applicable.
clinicalQuestion: Does adjuvant sorafenib reduce recurrence after nephrectomy for intermediate/high-risk RCC?
refs: Eisen T, et al. J Clin Oncol. 2020;38:4064–4075.

treatment: Abiraterone + prednisolone with standard androgen deprivation vs standard therapy
population: 1,974 men with high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer in STAMPEDE randomized comparisons
benefitText: Adding abiraterone plus prednisolone to standard therapy increased 6-year OS from 77% to 86%, an absolute benefit of 9 points (NNT 12). The benefit was large and consistent across major subgroups. NNT is based on 6-year overall survival.
nnH: Not quantified here; hypertension, liver abnormalities and other treatment-related toxicities should be reported in text
trial: STAMPEDE abiraterone in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer
clinicalQuestion: Should abiraterone be added to standard androgen-deprivation-based treatment for high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer?
refs: Attard G, et al. Lancet. 2022;399:447–460.

treatment: Enzalutamide + leuprolide or enzalutamide monotherapy vs leuprolide alone
population: 1,068 men with high-risk biochemical recurrence after definitive local therapy
benefitText: Five-year metastasis-free survival was 87.3% with enzalutamide plus leuprolide vs 71.4% with leuprolide alone, an absolute improvement of 15.9 points (NNT 7). Enzalutamide monotherapy also improved MFS to 80.0%, ARR 8.6 points. NNT is based on 5-year MFS.
nnH: Not quantified here because the main publication did not provide a single clinically dominant toxicity endpoint suitable for an NNH
clinicalQuestion: In high-risk biochemical recurrence, can enzalutamide delay metastasis compared with conventional ADT?
refs: Freedland SJ, et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:1459–1471.

treatment: [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 + standard treatment vs standard treatment
population: PSMA-positive metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
nnt: Not calculated from median-only survival data
ci: Phase III PSMAddition; exact fixed-time absolute effect should be reported from the primary publication
benefitText: PSMAddition established a theranostic strategy in PSMA-positive metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: adding radioligand therapy to standard treatment significantly prolonged radiographic PFS. Because the principal published result is a time-to-event effect rather than a clean fixed-time absolute event rate, NNT is not calculated here. The entry is deliberately classified under the Theranostic Trials setting.
nnH: Not quantified here; hematologic and other radioligand-related toxicities should be reported from the full safety analysis
clinicalQuestion: Does PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy add meaningful benefit to standard treatment in PSMA-positive metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer?
refs: Hofman MS, et al. PSMAddition phase III trial.
